spoken: Imagine a party with 23 guests.
What are the chances that two of them share a birthday?
With 365 days in a year, a match sounds unlikely.
In fact, it's more likely than not. The chance is 50.7 percent.
With 70 guests, it's 99.9 percent, which is almost certain.
This is the birthday problem. Let's see why it works.
First, here are the rules of our party.
Each birthday is one of 365 days, all equally likely, and we'll leave out February the twenty-ninth.
Guests arrive one at a time, and we mark each birthday on the calendar.
Guest 20 lands on a day that's already taken. It's November the nineteenth, the birthday of guest 7.
That's one party. Here are 1,000 more, each with 23 random guests.
511 of them have a shared birthday. That's about half, just as the maths says.
Our instincts say it should take far more guests. In one study, most people markedly overestimated the number needed.
The puzzle is usually credited to the mathematician Harold Davenport, around 1927.
He didn't publish it, or claim it as his own, because he couldn't believe nobody had stated it before.
The first published version came from Richard von Meezes, in 1939.
So why does our intuition get this so wrong?
It's natural to think about your own birthday.
With 22 other guests, the chance that someone shares yours is only about 6 percent.
But any two guests can make a match, not just you and someone else.
So draw a line between every pair of guests.
The first guest pairs with 22 others, the next with 21 more, and so on.
That's 23 times 22, divided by 2, which makes 253 pairs.
Only 22 of those pairs include you. The other 231 are matches you weren't counting.
And pairs grow fast. Double the guests to 46, and there are 1,035 pairs, which is about four times as many.
For the exact chance, it's easier to work out the opposite, which is that no two guests share a birthday.
The first guest can have any birthday, so that's 365 days out of 365.
The second must miss the first, so it's 364 out of 365.
The third must miss both, which leaves 363 out of 365, and so on.
Guest 23 must miss all 22 before, which leaves 343 out of 365.
Multiply all 23 fractions, and the chance that every birthday differs is 49.3 percent.
So the chance of at least one shared birthday is 50.7 percent.
Each fraction is close to 1, but there are many, and each new guest has more birthdays to avoid.
Do the same sum for every size of party, and the chance climbs quickly.
With 10 guests, the chance is 11.7 percent; with 30, it's 70.6 percent; with 50, it's 97 percent.
It passes 99 percent at 57 guests, and 99.9 percent at 70.
A match is only certain at 366 guests, when there are more guests than days.
Let's watch it happen. Guests enter a room one by one, and we stop at the first shared birthday.
In this room, the first match came with guest 28.
In this one, it came with guest 33, and in this one, with guest 18.
Now let's try a thousand rooms. Each dot is one room, placed at the guest who brought its first match.
A few rooms matched very early, with just 3 guests. A few went past 60.
In 511 of the 1,000 rooms, the first match came by guest 23.
On average, the first match took 24.7 guests. The theory says about 24.6.
Real groups behave the same way. At the 2014 World Cup, each of the 32 squads had 23 players.
An analysis of the squad lists suggested that 16 of them had a shared birthday, which is exactly half.
Five of those squads even had two pairs.
Now change the question. How many people do you need for an even chance that someone shares your birthday?
Each person matches you with a chance of one in 365.
So the chance that nobody does is 364 out of 365, multiplied once for every person.
That shrinks slowly. It takes 253 people to reach an even chance.
That's far more than half of 365, because many of those people share birthdays with each other instead.
Drop 253 random birthdays on the calendar, and they land on only 180 different days.
So your birthday has only about an even chance of being one of them.
Now look at that number again. 253 is exactly the number of pairs among 23 guests.
That's no coincidence. Both questions need about 253 chances, each of one in 365.
A one-in-365 chance becomes an even bet after about 253 tries. That's 365 times the natural log of 2.
That gives a quick rule for any number of days, not just 365.
With n guests, there are about n squared over 2 pairs.
For an even chance we need about 253 pairs, so n squared should be about 506.
The square root of 506 is about 22.5. Round up, and you get 23.
In general, you need about 1.18 times the square root of the number of days.
With a million equally likely days, just 1,178 people would give an even chance.
The real surprise is that the people needed grow only like the square root of the days.
Our party made some simplifications. It had 365 equally likely days, no February the twenty-ninth, and no twins.
Real birthdays aren't spread evenly. In the United States, more babies tend to be born in September and October.
From 1973 to 1999, September the sixteenth was the most common birthday in the United States, and Christmas Day the rarest, apart from February the twenty-ninth.
Does that break the maths? No, any unevenness only makes a shared birthday more likely.
Take an extreme case, and imagine everyone was born in the first half of the year.
Then just 17 guests would give a better-than-even chance.
Real birthdays are only slightly uneven, so the real-world answer is still 23.
And twins nearly always share a birthday, which can only raise the chance.
The same maths matters in computer security.
A hash function turns any file into a short digital fingerprint of fixed length.
A 64-bit fingerprint has about 18 billion billion possible values.
Two different files with the same fingerprint make a collision.
Fingerprints are like birthdays, in a year with an enormous number of days.
So collisions show up after about the square root of that number. That's 2 to the power of half the number of bits.
For 64 bits, about 5 billion tries give an even chance of a collision.
Matching one particular fingerprint, like matching your own birthday, takes about 13 billion billion tries.
That's the idea behind the birthday attack. Imagine a forger with a fair contract and a fraudulent one.
She makes many harmless variations of each, such as an extra comma, a double space or a synonym.
When a fair version and a fraudulent version share a fingerprint, she has her collision.
Her victim signs the fair version, and the signature fits the fraudulent one just as well.
The defence is longer fingerprints, with about twice as many bits as brute force alone would demand.
S H A 256 has 256 bits, so a collision takes around 2 to the power of 128 tries. That's a number with 39 digits.
So, let's go back to the party.
23 guests sound like too few, because we picture matches with ourselves.
But every pair is a chance, and 23 guests make 253 pairs.
That's enough for a better-than-even chance of 50.7 percent.
So next time you're in a room of 23 people or more, ask around.
More often than not, two of you will share a birthday.
